pos: n. (a graduated instrument marking the sun's shadow; the dial of Ahaz, on which the shadow went backward as a sign to Hezekiah)
etymology: From Latin dies, a day, through medieval Latin dialis. The Hebrew is maalah, a step or degree — the instrument was most likely a stair, and the shadow climbed or descended its steps.
biblical_def: Hezekiah, recovered from a mortal sickness, asked for a sign, and Isaiah offered him a choice: “This sign shalt thou have of the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?” (2 Kings 20:9). The king's reply shows he understood the difference: “It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees” (2 Kings 20:10). Forward is what shadows do; backward is not. “And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of Ahaz” (2 Kings 20:11). Isaiah records the same event with an added detail: “So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down” (Isaiah 38:8). Two things are worth noticing. The instrument is named for Ahaz, Hezekiah's idolatrous father, so the sign was given on a device built by a wicked king. And the sign runs backward — the direction time does not go — to confirm a promise of fifteen added years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dial as an instrument for measuring time by the sun's shadow, consisting of a plate with lines and a gnomon or style.
webster_full: DIAL, n. An instrument for measuring time by the aid of the sun; being a plate or plain surface, on which lines are drawn.
2. The plate of a clock or watch on which the hours are marked.
GNOMON, n. In dialing, the style or pin which by its shadow shows the hour of the day.
DEGREE, n. A step; a division of a line or space marked on an instrument.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane.
scriptures: 2 Kings 20:11
And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of Ahaz.
Isaiah 38:8
Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down.
2 Kings 20:9
And Isaiah said, This sign shalt thou have of the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?
2 Kings 20:10
And Hezekiah answered, It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees.
corruption_summary: The miracle is explained away as an optical curiosity, and the sign's point — a God who commands the shadow — is lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard treatment of this passage in critical commentary is to find a natural mechanism — a refraction, an eclipse, a local atmospheric effect — or to file the whole account as a later embellishment. Both moves assume in advance that the event as narrated cannot have occurred, which is the assumption itself and not a conclusion from evidence. The text is careful in a way that resists the reduction: Hezekiah is offered a choice, he reasons about which direction would constitute a sign, and he deliberately asks for the harder one. A narrative shaped to record an optical illusion would not include a king weighing which illusion to request.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's freedom over the order He established. Scripture never treats the regularity of creation as a limit on its Maker; the same God who appointed the sun to rule the day moved its shadow backward on a stairway in Jerusalem. This is why the resurrection is not, in biblical terms, an oddity requiring special pleading — it belongs to a God who has always dealt with His creation this way. The 1689 Confession states it: God in His ordinary providence makes use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them at His pleasure. The dial of Ahaz is that clause in a single afternoon.
roots_summary: Hebrew maalah, a step or degree — 2 Kings 20:9-11, Isaiah 38:8; tsel, a shadow — same passages; the instrument is called the degrees or steps of Ahaz.
roots_lines: Hebrew maalah — a step, stair, degree; rendered degrees and, in the construction, dial; the same word titles the Songs of Degrees.
Hebrew tsel — shadow; 2 Kings 20:9-11, the thing that moved.
Hebrew Ahaz — Hezekiah's father, an idolatrous king; the dial bore his name.
Hebrew oth — a sign; 2 Kings 20:9, what Hezekiah was given.
2 Chronicles 32:31 notes that the ambassadors of Babylon came to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land.
usage: “He brought the shadow ten degrees backward” — the direction shadows do not go.
“It is a light thing for the shadow to go down” — Hezekiah asked for the harder sign.
The sign was given on an instrument built by a wicked king.

pos: adj. (split, divided; of the parted hoof that marks a clean beast, and of the tongues of fire at Pentecost)
etymology: Past participle of cleave, Old English cleofan, to split. The Greek in Acts 2:3 is diamerizo, to divide or distribute — tongues that parted and distributed themselves.
biblical_def: The word belongs first to the law of clean and unclean beasts. The rule requires two marks together: “Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat” (Leviticus 11:3), and Deuteronomy names the animals that have one mark without the other — “these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you” (Deuteronomy 14:7). Half the marks was not enough. The second and greater use is at Pentecost: “And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them” (Acts 2:3). The tongues divided and came to rest on individuals, one apiece — the Spirit distributed, not poured on the assembly as an undifferentiated mass. And the result was tongues in the other sense: “they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). Fire divides in Acts 2 in order to gather; the confusion of Babel begins to be undone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cloven as divided or parted, and cloven-footed as having the foot or hoof divided into two parts, as the ox.
webster_full: CLOVEN, pp. of cleave. Divided; parted; split.
CLOVEN-FOOTED, CLOVEN-HOOFED, a. Having the foot or hoof divided into two parts, as the ox.
CLEAVE, v.t. To part or divide by force; to split or rive.
CUD, n. The food which ruminating animals bring up from the first stomach to chew a second time.
UNCLEAN, a. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; forbidden by the law to be eaten.
scriptures: Acts 2:3
And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them.
Acts 2:4
And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
Deuteronomy 14:7

Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you.
Leviticus 11:3
Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat.
corruption_summary: Pentecost is turned into a template for repeatable experience, and the dietary law is either dismissed as arbitrary or reimposed on the conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 2 records an unrepeatable event. The tongues of fire, the rushing mighty wind and the speaking in the languages of the assembled nations belong to the once-for-all inauguration of the new covenant era, as the crucifixion and resurrection do. Modern movements that treat the chapter as a pattern to be reproduced — and that make a particular subsequent experience the mark of a true believer — have made a narrative into a norm. Peter's own sermon interprets the day as the fulfilment of Joel and the enthronement of Christ, not as the first of a series of identical occurrences. The cessationist position the Reformed churches have held is not a diminishing of the Spirit but a refusal to demand from Him what He did not promise to repeat.

The dietary law is misused from both ends. One error treats the clean and unclean distinctions as arbitrary taboos with no meaning, forgetting that God gave the reason in Leviticus 11:44 — be ye holy, for I am holy — and that the marks taught Israel to be a separated people in the most ordinary act of every day. The other error reimposes the food laws on Christians, which Mark 7:19 and Acts 10 and Colossians 2:16 forbid. The shadow taught a real lesson and the body is of Christ. What remains permanently is the principle the cloven hoof illustrated: half a mark is not enough, and God distinguishes.
roots_summary: Hebrew shasa, to split — Leviticus 11:3, Deuteronomy 14:7; Greek diamerizo (G1266), to divide or distribute — Acts 2:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew shasa — to split, to cleave; the cloven hoof of Leviticus 11:3 and Deuteronomy 14:7.
Hebrew parsah — a hoof; the part that must be parted for a beast to be clean.
Greek diamerizo (G1266) — to divide, to distribute; Acts 2:3, of the tongues that parted.
Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue; used in Acts 2 both of the flames and of the languages spoken.
Leviticus 11:44 gives the reason behind the marks: ye shall be holy; for I am holy.
usage: “Cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them” — distributed, one apiece.
“They chew the cud, but divide not the hoof” — half a mark was not enough.
Fire divides at Pentecost in order to gather.

pos: n. pl. (money-changers; the temple exchange whose tables the Lord overthrew)
etymology: From change, Latin cambiare, to barter. The Greek in John 2:14 is kermatistes, a dealer in small coin, and in verse 15 kollubistes, from the kollubos or exchange fee — the commission is built into the name.
biblical_def: “And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting” (John 2:14). Their trade was necessary in itself: pilgrims arrived with foreign coin bearing pagan images, and the temple tax had to be paid in acceptable currency. The offence was the place and the profit. “And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables” (John 2:15). His stated charge is not fraud but commerce: “Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (John 2:16). At the second cleansing, near the end of His ministry, Matthew records that He “overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves” (Matthew 21:12), and there He quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah — a house of prayer made a den of thieves. The doves matter: they were the offering of the poor, and the poor were paying a markup to worship. The scourge was made by hand, of small cords, which means it was made deliberately and not in a moment's temper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a changer as one that changes, and a money-changer as a broker who deals in the exchange of money.
webster_full: CHANGER, n. One that alters the form of any thing.
2. One that is employed in changing and discounting money; a money-changer.
EXCHANGE, n. The act of giving one thing or commodity for another.
MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
TABLE, n. A frame or board on which money is counted; the counter of a money-changer.
scriptures: John 2:14
And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting:
John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
John 2:16
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
Matthew 21:12
And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,
corruption_summary: The cleansing is quoted against every commercial abuse except the one it names — selling access to worship, especially to the poor.
corruption_paragraphs: The episode is a favourite text for sermons against greed in general, and its actual target is narrower and closer to home: a religious establishment monetising access to the worship of God. The changers were not con men operating outside the system; they were licensed, necessary, and inside the temple precincts, and the doves they sold were the offering the law appointed for those who could not afford a lamb. That is the arrangement Christ overturned with a scourge He took the time to make. Any ministry that puts a price between a poor worshipper and the God he came to worship — a conference fee, a course, a giving level attached to standing — is standing at the changers' table, whatever its accounting is like.

The second misuse is the appeal to this passage to justify anger, as though the scene licensed the sharp temper a man has already decided to indulge. Note the details John supplies. The scourge was made of small cords, by hand, which takes time; the doves were told to be taken out rather than released, since driving them off would have destroyed the property of men who were not the principal offenders; and the charge given is a sentence of doctrine, not an insult. This is judicial action by the Son in His Father's house, not a loss of composure, and the man who cites it for his own outbursts has borrowed the wrong precedent.
roots_summary: Greek kermatistes (G2773), a money-changer — John 2:14, its only occurrence; kollubistes (G2855), an exchanger — John 2:15, Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15; emporion (G1712), a house of merchandise — John 2:16.
roots_lines: Greek kermatistes (G2773) — a dealer in small change; John 2:14, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek kollubistes (G2855) — an exchanger, named from the kollubos or commission; John 2:15, Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15.
Greek emporion (G1712) — a place of merchandise, a market; John 2:16, its only occurrence.
Greek phragellion (G5416) — a scourge of cords; John 2:15, its only occurrence, and made by hand.
John 2:17 records the disciples' recollection: the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
usage: “Poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables” — the trade was licensed and inside the precincts.
“Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” — the charge is commerce, not fraud.
The scourge was made of small cords, which takes time.

pos: n. (a cleansing alkali; in Jeremiah the futility of self-washing, and in Malachi a figure of the refining Christ)
etymology: Old English sape. The Hebrew borith is a vegetable alkali or lye used by fullers in cleaning cloth — a harsh industrial cleanser, not a toilet article, which is why both prophetic uses are severe.
biblical_def: Jeremiah uses it to close off an escape: “For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord GOD” (Jeremiah 2:22). Two cleansers are named, the strongest available, and used in quantity — and the stain remains. The verse is one of the plainest statements in the Old Testament that sin is not removed by any effort of the sinner's own; the mark is before God, and no amount of scrubbing reaches it. Malachi takes the same substance and puts it in the hands of the Coming One: “But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap” (Malachi 3:2). What a man cannot do to himself, the Messenger of the covenant does to him — and the next verse says where He begins: “he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness” (Malachi 3:3). Judgment starts with the ministers. Isaiah states the promise the two prophets frame: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soap as a compound of oil with an alkali, used in washing and cleansing, and fuller as one whose occupation is to full and cleanse cloth.
webster_full: SOAP, n. A compound of oil and alkali, used in washing and cleansing.
FULLER, n. One whose occupation is to full and cleanse cloth.
FULLER'S EARTH, a variety of clay, so called from its use in scouring and cleansing cloth.
NITRE, n. A salt; in the ancient sense, a natural alkali used in washing.
REFINE, v.t. To purify; to separate from extraneous matter, as metals from dross.
scriptures: Jeremiah 2:22
For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord GOD.
Malachi 3:2
But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:
Malachi 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.
Isaiah 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
corruption_summary: Cleansing is treated as something a man performs on himself by reform, and Jeremiah says the strongest soap available will not touch the stain.
corruption_paragraphs: Every religion of self-improvement is answered by Jeremiah 2:22. The prophet grants the effort — much soap, the best cleansers of the trade, applied in quantity — and denies the result, because the iniquity is marked before me, and the stain is in a place the sinner cannot reach. Moral reformation is a good thing and it is not cleansing; a man may change his conduct entirely and stand exactly as guilty as before, since guilt is a relation to God and not a habit. This is the doctrine that makes the gospel necessary rather than merely helpful, and it is the doctrine most quietly abandoned in preaching that treats Christianity as a programme of improvement.

Malachi 3 supplies the corrective and it is not comfortable either. The cleansing comes, and it comes as a refiner's fire and fullers' soap — a harsh alkali beaten into cloth, and metal held in the heat until the dross rises. The question who may abide the day of his coming is asked of a people who had been demanding that the LORD come and set things right. He answers that He will come, and begin with the priesthood. Any church that longs for God to deal with the corruption of the age should read the next verse before praying it again: He sits down at the refiner's furnace, and He purifies the sons of Levi first.
roots_summary: Hebrew borith, lye or soap — Jeremiah 2:22, Malachi 3:2; nether, nitre or natural alkali — Jeremiah 2:22, Proverbs 25:20.
roots_lines: Hebrew borith — a vegetable alkali used by fullers; Jeremiah 2:22 and Malachi 3:2, its only occurrences.
Hebrew nether — nitre, a natural alkali; Jeremiah 2:22, paired with soap as the strongest cleanser available.
Hebrew kabas — to wash by treading, the fuller's trade; the verb behind the imagery.
Hebrew tsaraph — to refine, to smelt; Malachi 3:2-3, the refiner and purifier of silver.
Malachi 3:1 names the one who comes: the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple.
usage: “Though thou… take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me”.
“Like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap” — both are harsh, and both are effective.
“He shall purify the sons of Levi” — the cleansing begins with the ministers.

pos: n. (a basin for washing the feet; in Psalms 60 and 108, a figure of Moab's subjection)
etymology: From wash and pot, rendering Hebrew sir rachats, a pot for washing. In a household the washpot was the basin set out for the feet of guests — the humblest vessel in the room, handled by the lowest servant.
biblical_def: “Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me” (Psalm 60:8), repeated almost exactly in Psalm 108:9. The oracle is God's own speech in the middle of the psalm, and it follows a roll-call of Israel's own tribes: “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver” (Psalm 60:7). Then the neighbouring nations, and the imagery drops sharply. Moab — a nation descended from Lot, long hostile — is the basin a man washes his feet in. Edom is where he throws his dirty sandal. These are deliberately humiliating figures, and they are not boasts by Israel; they are declarations by the LORD about His own disposal of the nations. The psalm is set in a time of defeat — “O God, thou hast cast us off” is its opening — so the oracle functions as reassurance: the God who seems to have abandoned His people still holds Moab as a footbasin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a washpot as a vessel in which any thing is washed, and notes the biblical figure of contempt.
webster_full: WASH-POT, n. A vessel in which any thing is washed.
BASIN, n. A hollow vessel or dish, to hold water for washing.
SUBJECTION, n. The act of subduing; the act of vanquishing and bringing under the dominion of another.
CONTEMPT, n. The act of despising; the act of viewing or considering and treating as mean, vile and worthless.
SHOE, n. A covering for the foot, usually of leather.
scriptures: Psalm 60:8
Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me.
Psalm 108:9
Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe; over Philistia will I triumph.
Psalm 60:7
Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver;
Lamentations 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
corruption_summary: The imprecatory and triumphal psalms are edited out of worship for their harshness, and the congregation loses the psalter's realism about nations and enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 60:8 is the kind of verse that never appears on a wall. Its imagery is contemptuous by design, and modern worship has largely solved the problem by singing only the psalms that suit a gentle register. The result is a church that sings a third of the psalter and reads the rest with embarrassment. But the psalms were given as the songbook of the covenant people, and they include defeat, complaint, imprecation and triumph because the people who sing them live in a world that contains all four. Removing the difficult psalms does not make the difficulties go away; it leaves the congregation without inspired words for half its actual experience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's setting. These triumphant lines about Moab and Edom are spoken in a psalm that opens O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us. The oracle is not gloating from a position of strength; it is God's word to a defeated people, reminding them who actually holds the nations while their own army is broken. That is how the passage should be preached — not as a licence for national contempt, which the Old Testament itself condemns in Edom's case, but as the sovereignty of God asserted at the worst possible moment.
roots_summary: Hebrew sir rachats, a pot for washing — Psalm 60:8, 108:9; naal, a sandal or shoe — same verses; Moab and Edom, the two neighbouring nations named.
roots_lines: Hebrew sir — a pot or basin; joined with rachats, to wash, in the figure of Psalm 60:8.
Hebrew rachats — to wash, especially the feet; the humblest household service.
Hebrew naal — a sandal; casting out the shoe over a land signified possession or contempt, as in Ruth 4:7.
Hebrew Moab — the nation descended from Lot, and Ruth's own people.
Psalm 60:11-12 closes the psalm where its confidence rests: give us help from trouble, for vain is the help of man.
usage: “Moab is my washpot” — the basin for the feet, the humblest vessel in the house.
“Over Edom will I cast out my shoe” — a gesture of possession and contempt.
The oracle is spoken to a people who have just been defeated.

pos: n. pl. (natural springs of water; in Psalm 107 the emblem of God's power to reverse a land's fortunes either way)
etymology: From water and spring, rendering Hebrew motsa mayim, an outgoing or source of water. A spring in that country was not a convenience but the difference between a settlement and a desert.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice in one psalm, in two verses that are exact mirrors. First the drying: “He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground” (Psalm 107:33), and the reason is given in the next verse — “A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein” (Psalm 107:34). Then the reverse: “He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings” (Psalm 107:35), and there too the sequel is given — “And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation” (Psalm 107:36). The same verb, the same God, opposite directions. The psalm has spent its earlier stanzas on four groups delivered from four distresses — the lost, the imprisoned, the sick and the storm-tossed — each with the refrain Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness. These two verses generalise the pattern to geography itself. Fertility and desolation are not simply the weather; they are the acts of the God who governs both, and the psalm ends by saying that whoso is wise will observe these things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a spring as a fountain of water, an issue of water from the earth, and the source or head of a stream.
webster_full: SPRING, n. A fountain of water; an issue of water from the earth, or the basin of water at the place of its issue.
2. The source of anything; that from which a thing proceeds.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
BARRENNESS, n. The quality of not producing its kind; want of the power of conception; sterility.
HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode.
scriptures: Psalm 107:33
He turneth rivers into a wilderness, and the watersprings into dry ground;
Psalm 107:35
He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings.
Psalm 107:34
A fruitful land into barrenness, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein.
Psalm 107:36
And there he maketh the hungry to dwell, that they may prepare a city for habitation;
corruption_summary: Land and weather are removed from providence altogether, or else read as a simple scorecard of a nation's righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 107:34 says a fruitful land is turned to barrenness for the wickedness of them that dwell therein, and there are two ways to get this wrong. The first is to deny that God has anything to do with the physical fortunes of a place, which the psalm plainly asserts that He does. The second, and the one more common among people who take the verse seriously, is to reverse it into a diagnostic tool — reading every drought and every disaster as a decoded message about a particular sin. Our Lord forbade exactly that inference about the tower of Siloam and the Galileans, and Job's comforters were rebuked for practising it. God governs the rain; He has not licensed anyone to publish the reasons.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's symmetry, which is a comfort more than a threat. The God who dries up the springs is the God who turns the wilderness into standing water, and He does the second for the hungry, so that they may prepare a city. The reversals run both directions and the second is the direction the psalm ends on. A congregation looking at a dry season — in a family, a ministry, a nation — is being told by verse 35 that the same hand which emptied the spring can open one in a desert, and by verse 43 that the wise will watch for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew motsa mayim, a spring or outgoing of water — Psalm 107:33, 107:35; midbar, wilderness; tsimmaon, thirsty ground.
roots_lines: Hebrew motsa — a going forth, a source; joined with mayim, water, for the springs of Psalm 107:33, 35.
Hebrew midbar — wilderness, uninhabited pasture land; the term the psalm moves in both directions.
Hebrew melechah — saltness, barrenness; Psalm 107:34, of the fruitful land turned.
Hebrew agam mayim — a pool or standing water; Psalm 107:35, the wilderness reversed.
Psalm 107:43 closes the psalm: whoso is wise, and will observe these things, even they shall understand the lovingkindness of the LORD.
usage: “He turneth… the watersprings into dry ground” — and the reason follows in the next verse.
“He turneth the wilderness into a standing water” — the same verb, the other direction.
“There he maketh the hungry to dwell” — the reversal is for somebody.

pos: n. (a channel cut for water; used of Hezekiah's conduit at Gihon and of the channel God cuts for the rain)
etymology: From water and course, Latin cursus, a running. The Hebrew in Job 38:25 is teala, a conduit or trench; in 2 Chronicles 32:30 the term describes an engineered channel.
biblical_def: The word describes engineering, human and divine. Hezekiah, facing the Assyrian siege, cut off the water supply outside the city and brought it within: “This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works” (2 Chronicles 32:30). Kings records the same works — “how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city” (2 Kings 20:20) — and the tunnel he drove through rock still runs under Jerusalem. The other use is God's, in the whirlwind speech: “Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder” (Job 38:25). The question is one of a long series designed to show Job how little of the world he made or manages. What follows is startling: God cuts these channels “To cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, wherein there is no man” (Job 38:26). Rain falls on ground no one will ever farm. The world is not built solely for human use, and that is part of the answer Job receives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a watercourse as a stream of water, a channel or canal for the conveyance of water, and a conduit as a canal or pipe for conveying water.
webster_full: WATER-COURSE, n. A stream of water; a channel or canal for the conveyance of water, particularly in draining lands.
CONDUIT, n. A canal or pipe for the conveyance of water; an aqueduct.
CHANNEL, n. The hollow bed of a river or other running stream of water.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
AQUEDUCT, n. A conductor of water; a construction of stone or wood for conveying water.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 32:30
This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.
Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder;
To cause it to rain on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, wherein there is no man;
2 Kings 20:20

And the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
corruption_summary: Trusting God and doing the work are treated as rivals, and Hezekiah did both in the same chapter.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 32 records Hezekiah stopping the springs, building the wall, making darts and shields, appointing captains, and cutting a tunnel through solid rock — and in the same chapter praying with Isaiah, and watching the angel of the LORD destroy the Assyrian army overnight. He is not presented as a man whose engineering showed weak faith, nor as one whose faith made the engineering unnecessary. The false alternative between trusting providence and using means is refuted by the whole narrative, and stated doctrinally in the Confession: God ordinarily works by means, though He is free to work without them. The tunnel and the angel belong to the same account.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in Job 38:26, which is one of the most quietly devastating verses in Scripture for a man-centred reading of creation. God divides a watercourse to send rain on the wilderness wherein there is no man. Nobody sees it; nobody benefits; it waters ground that will never be farmed. The utilitarian assumption that creation exists for human consumption cannot survive that sentence, and neither can the sentimental one that everything happens for our benefit. The world is God's, and much of what He does in it He does for His own glory with no audience at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew teala, a conduit or trench — Job 38:25, 2 Kings 18:17, 1 Kings 18:32; the engineered channel of 2 Chronicles 32:30; Gihon, the spring outside Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Hebrew teala — a watercourse, conduit, trench; Job 38:25, and the trench Elijah dug about the altar at Carmel.
Hebrew Gihon — the spring in the Kidron valley; 2 Chronicles 32:30, and where Solomon was anointed king.
Hebrew satham — to stop up; 2 Chronicles 32:30, of the springs Hezekiah closed against the Assyrians.
Hebrew berekah — a pool; 2 Kings 20:20, the pool of Siloam at the tunnel's outlet.
2 Chronicles 32:31 supplies the sequel, and the warning: God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
usage: “Stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down” — and prayed in the same chapter.
“Who hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters?” — the divine engineering.
“To cause it to rain… on the wilderness, wherein there is no man”.

pos: n. pl. (in Judges 3, the place by Gilgal where Ehud turned back and afterwards escaped; the margin reads graven images)
etymology: From Old French quarriere, a place where stone is cut. The Hebrew pesilim more properly means carved or graven images, which the Authorized Version's margin notes; the two senses meet in cut stone.
biblical_def: The word frames the strangest assassination in Scripture. Ehud, having delivered Israel's tribute to Eglon king of Moab, sent the bearers away: “But he himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal, and said, I have a secret errand unto thee, O king: who said, Keep silence. And all that stood by him went out from him” (Judges 3:19). He came in to the king in his summer parlour: “And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat” (Judges 3:20) — and the message was a dagger. Afterwards the same landmark marks his escape: “And Ehud escaped while they tarried, and passed beyond the quarries, and escaped unto Seirath” (Judges 3:26). The place is named twice and is the hinge of the story both times, and the location matters. Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the land and set up twelve stones from Jordan — and by the time of Judges there were pesilim there, graven images. The deliverer turned back at the idols to go and kill the oppressor whose dominion those idols represented.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a quarry as a place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, and notes the scriptural marginal sense of graven images.
webster_full: QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
2. In the Scriptures, the margin reads graven images.
GRAVEN, pp. of grave. Carved; engraved; cut with a chisel or graver.
TRIBUTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another, either for peace or protection.
DELIVERER, n. One who delivers; one who releases or rescues; a preserver.
scriptures: Judges 3:19
But he himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal, and said, I have a secret errand unto thee, O king: who said, Keep silence. And all that stood by him went out from him.
Judges 3:26
And Ehud escaped while they tarried, and passed beyond the quarries, and escaped unto Seirath.
Judges 3:20
And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat.
Exodus 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
corruption_summary: Judges is read either as a gallery of heroes to imitate or as material too violent to preach, and the book's own verdict on the period is skipped.
corruption_paragraphs: Ehud is not offered as a model of conduct, and the book of Judges is not a collection of moral examples. It is the record of a nation in a spiral, and its refrain — every man did that which was right in his own eyes — is a condemnation, not a description of liberty. Children's curricula that turn these narratives into hero stories, and pulpits that avoid them because of the violence, make opposite mistakes about the same book. God raised up deliverers who were flawed, sometimes badly, and Hebrews 11 lists several of them among the faithful without cleaning up their records. That is the doctrine of grace applied to history, and it is why the chapter can name Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah in one breath.

The location repays attention. The pesilim by Gilgal — graven images, as the margin has it — stood at the very place where Israel had first memorialised the crossing of Jordan with twelve stones taken from the riverbed. Within a few generations the site of the memorial was a site of idols. That is how quickly a monument to God's faithfulness becomes furniture for false worship, and it is the second commandment's own warning in narrative form. Ehud turned back at those stones to strike the king whose eighteen-year dominion was the fruit of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesilim, graven images — Judges 3:19, 3:26, and the Authorized Version's marginal reading; from pasal, to hew or carve; Gilgal, the first camp in the land.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesilim — graven images; Judges 3:19 and 3:26, rendered quarries with the margin noting the other sense.
Hebrew pasal — to hew, to carve; the root, used of the tables of stone Moses hewed in Exodus 34:1.
Hebrew Gilgal — a rolling; Joshua 4:20, where the twelve stones from Jordan were set up.
Hebrew Eglon — the king of Moab whose dominion over Israel lasted eighteen years, Judges 3:14.
Judges 3:15 introduces the deliverer: Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded.
usage: “He himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal” — the hinge of the story.
“Passed beyond the quarries, and escaped unto Seirath” — the same landmark on the way out.
Graven images stood where the memorial stones had been set up.

pos: n. (the outer defensive mound or bulwark of a fortified city; in Lamentations made to mourn, and in Nahum shown to be no defence at all)
etymology: French rempart, from remparer, to fortify. The Hebrew chel denotes the outer rampart or fore-wall, the earthwork standing before the wall proper — the first line, not the last.
biblical_def: Lamentations personifies the defences of a doomed city: “The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together” (Lamentations 2:8). Two things stand out. The destroyer is named — the LORD purposed it, and stretched out the measuring line, which is the builder's instrument turned to demolition. And the fortifications themselves mourn. Nahum makes the argument explicit against Nineveh by pointing at an earlier casualty: “Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?” (Nahum 3:8). Thebes had the best rampart imaginable — the Nile itself — and Ethiopia and Egypt for allies, “and it was infinite” (Nahum 3:9), and Thebes fell. The argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if that city could not stand, Nineveh cannot. No earthwork is a defence when the LORD has stretched out the line.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rampart as an elevation of earth round a place, serving to cover it from the fire of an enemy, and a bulwark as a rampart or fortification.
webster_full: RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
2. That which fortifies and defends from assault; that which secures safety.
BULWARK, n. In fortification, a bastion, or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot.
FORTIFY, v.t. To surround with a wall, ditch, palisades or other works, with a view to defend against the attacks of an enemy.
LANGUISH, v.i. To lose strength or animation; to be or to become dull, feeble or spiritless.
scriptures: Lamentations 2:8

The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together.
Nahum 3:8
Art thou better than populous No, that was situate among the rivers, that had the waters round about it, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was from the sea?
Nahum 3:9
Ethiopia and Egypt were her strength, and it was infinite; Put and Lubim were thy helpers.
Lamentations 2:9
Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: the law is no more; her prophets also find no vision from the LORD.
corruption_summary: Security is sought in the defences themselves, and Lamentations names the LORD as the one who purposed their fall.
corruption_paragraphs: Lamentations 2:8 is a hard verse for any theology that will not say God does the destroying. The prophet does not describe Babylon breaching a wall; he says the LORD hath purposed to destroy, and stretched out the line, and did not withdraw His hand. Modern treatments regularly soften this into permission — God allowed it, God did not prevent it — which is not what the text says and not what the Confession says either: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and is neither the author of sin nor a bystander to history. The men who broke that wall were wicked and were fully responsible; the purpose was the LORD's. Lamentations is written by someone who believed both and wept anyway.

The practical corruption is the one Nahum attacks: trusting the rampart. Thebes had the Nile for a moat and infinite allies, and fell. Nineveh had walls that were the wonder of the age, and fell within a generation of the prophecy. Every institution builds ramparts — endowments, reputations, legal protections, structures designed so that nothing can go badly wrong — and Scripture's consistent judgment is that these are exactly as strong as God permits and no stronger. Lamentations 2:9 shows what the fall of a rampart actually costs: the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision. That is the loss to grieve, and no earthwork ever protected it.
roots_summary: Hebrew chel, an outer rampart or fore-wall — Lamentations 2:8, Nahum 3:8, Psalm 122:7; chomah, the wall proper; No, the city of Thebes in Egypt.
roots_lines: Hebrew chel — a rampart, the outer fortification; Lamentations 2:8, Nahum 3:8, and Psalm 122:7 where peace is prayed within it.
Hebrew chomah — a city wall; paired with the rampart in Lamentations 2:8, and they languish together.
Hebrew qav — a measuring line; Lamentations 2:8, the builder's tool used for demolition.
Hebrew No — Thebes, the Egyptian capital on the Nile; Nahum 3:8, and Jeremiah 46:25.
Nahum 3:10 completes the argument: yet was she carried away, she went into captivity.
usage: “He made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together”.
“Whose rampart was the sea” — the best defence imaginable, and it fell.
“The LORD hath purposed to destroy” — not permitted; purposed.

pos: n. pl. (images or carved representations; commanded to be destroyed in Canaan, and used in Proverbs for the setting of a well-spoken word)
etymology: Latin pictura, a painting, from pingere, to paint. The Hebrew varies: maskith in Numbers 33:52 is a figured stone or carved image; in Proverbs 25:11 the same root gives a setting or filigree of silver.
biblical_def: The first use is a command of destruction: “Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you, and destroy all their pictures, and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places” (Numbers 33:52). Three objects, three verbs of demolition, and the whole apparatus of Canaanite worship is to go. Isaiah lists them among the objects of the day of the LORD: “And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all pleasant pictures” (Isaiah 2:16) — commerce and art alike brought low when human loftiness is judged. But the word is not condemned in itself, and Proverbs proves it with one of the loveliest images in the book: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). The picture there is a setting, a worked frame of silver holding golden fruit, and the whole point is the beauty of the arrangement. The next verse continues it: “As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear” (Proverbs 25:12). Craftsmanship and beauty are not the problem. Worship is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a picture as a painting exhibiting the resemblance of anything, and also any resemblance or representation.
webster_full: PICTURE, n. A painting exhibiting the resemblance of any thing; a likeness drawn in colors.
2. The works of painters; painting.
3. Any resemblance or representation, either to the eye or to the understanding.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.
2. An idol; the representation of any person or thing, that is an object of worship.
scriptures: Numbers 33:52
Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you, and destroy all their pictures, and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places:
Proverbs 25:11
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Isaiah 2:16
And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all pleasant pictures.
Proverbs 25:12
As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear.
corruption_summary: The second commandment is read either as a ban on art altogether or as a dead letter, and Scripture holds a narrower and more useful line.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 33:52 orders the destruction of images, and Proverbs 25:11 praises a worked setting of silver as a figure for good speech; the same Scriptures that command the smashing gave the pattern of the tabernacle in exhaustive artistic detail, with cherubim, pomegranates, blue and purple and scarlet, and named Bezaleel as filled with the Spirit of God in workmanship. The prohibition is not of representation but of representation for worship, and specifically of any image of God. The iconoclasm that treats all art as suspect has overshot the commandment; the Reformed tradition, which produced the Dutch masters and Bach, never held it.

The opposite corruption is the defence of images of Christ. The usual argument is that the incarnation makes it lawful to depict Him, since He took a real human nature. The Reformed churches have answered that the natures may not be divided: what is portrayed is the Person, and the Person is God, whom no man hath seen at any time. The Larger Catechism names images of God, of any of the three Persons, as forbidden by the second commandment. Whatever a believer concludes about art on a wall, the commandment's own scope is worship, and the pictures of Numbers 33 were destroyed for that reason and no other.
roots_summary: Hebrew maskith, a figured stone or carved image — Numbers 33:52, Leviticus 26:1; the same root for a setting or filigree — Proverbs 25:11; sekiyyah, imagery — Isaiah 2:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew maskith — a figure, an imagination, a carved stone; Numbers 33:52, Leviticus 26:1, and Proverbs 25:11 of a silver setting.
Hebrew massekah — a molten image; Numbers 33:52, the second of the three objects to be destroyed.
Hebrew bamah — a high place; Numbers 33:52, to be quite plucked down.
Hebrew sekiyyah — imagery, something looked at; Isaiah 2:16, the pleasant pictures brought low.
Exodus 31:3 shows the other side: Bezaleel filled with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in all manner of workmanship.
usage: “Destroy all their pictures… and quite pluck down all their high places” — the object is worship.
“Apples of gold in pictures of silver” — a worked setting, praised for its beauty.
The same law that forbade the images gave the pattern for the tabernacle.
